column4: Those who follow the unlettered Messenger find him written in earlier scripture, and he removes their burdens and shackles; preserved prophetic mention and relieved weight meet in the same portrait.
God will cast upon the Prophet a weighty word, a precise counterpoint to the section's claim that the back can carry sacred speech rather than an ordinary load.

Before the clear signs of 29:49 are held in learned breasts, the Prophet had neither recited a prior book nor written one by hand; the verse distinguishes inwardly received Quran from ordinary textual acquisition.
The Book sent to the Prophet must cause no constriction in his breast; he is to warn through it, and it is a reminder for believers, joining chest, scripture, and remembrance.
The Quran was not sent down to the Prophet so that he should suffer, setting revelation against oppressive weight before the next verse calls it a reminder.
The Quran of 20:2 is sent as a reminder for one who fears, giving the non-burdensome revelation its memory-making function.
After the promise that the Prophet will recite without forgetting, he is commanded to remind wherever the reminder benefits.
The Book sent to the Prophet is described as a clarification of everything, guidance, mercy, and good news, directly joining scripture with explanatory disclosure.
After an interval between messengers, the Messenger comes making matters clear so the People of the Book cannot claim that no bearer of news reached them.
The Merciful teaches the Quran, establishing the revealed object whose human articulation and explanation the following verses describe.
God teaches the human being clear expression, completing 55:2's Quran-teaching scene with the capacity for articulate explanation.
The narrative revelation confirms earlier scripture and gives a detailed exposition of all things, closely matching the source definition of zikir as a book containing religious detail.
People fold their breasts to hide from God, yet He knows what they conceal and disclose and what breasts contain; hidden interior and outward manifestation are joined at the chest.
In the People-of-the-Book passage, God knows both what they conceal and what they make public, directly framing their treatment of revelation as hidden versus disclosed.
God brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and earth and knows what people conceal and disclose, explicitly staging the emergence of the hidden.
The command is to remember the Lord inwardly, humbly, and below the level of loud speech; remembrance can be held within rather than circulated aloud on the tongue.
Believing hearts find rest through God's remembrance, locating zikir within the heart as something retained and sustaining.
Believers are commanded to remember God with abundant remembrance, directly exemplifying the section's dictionary gloss of zikrā as much remembering.
Men and women who remember God abundantly are named together, another exact Quranic realization of abundant remembrance.
Zechariah is commanded to remember his Lord much and glorify Him morning and evening, coupling prophetic speech with sustained remembrance.
Preventing God's name from being mentioned in His places of worship is the direct negative counterpart to houses raised for His name in 24:36.
Protected houses of worship are places in which God's name is mentioned abundantly, showing public remembrance preserved in built space.
When God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those denying the Hereafter recoil, while mention of others brings delight; spoken remembrance exposes inward reception.
A false companion leads a person away from the Reminder after it has reached him, another direct transition from present revelation to abandoned remembrance.
Those who turn back after guidance has become clear embody both movements at once: disclosure occurs, then the recipient places it behind him.
When God's signs are recited, the arrogant person turns away as though he had not heard, bodily enacting the refusal to retain spoken revelation.
The sinner hears God's signs recited yet persists as though he had not heard them, another exact image of a word reaching the ear but being discarded.
Whoever turns blindly away from the Merciful's remembrance is assigned a satanic companion, giving neglect of zikir a concrete consequence.
The two receiving recorders sit on the right and left, establishing the agents who preserve each person's otherwise passing acts.
No word is uttered without a watcher ready to record it, turning speech on the tongue into an enduring written account.
God's Book speaks against people in truth because their deeds were being copied, joining preserved record with public testimony.
God writes what people send ahead and the traces they leave, enumerating everything in a clear register; what passes is preserved and made legible.
Whether speech is voiced aloud or withheld, God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, applying the open-hidden movement specifically to words.
The Prophet is told not to hurry the Quran before its revelation is completed and to ask for increased knowledge, another boundary around faithful oral retention.
The Prophet is commanded to recite the Quran in a measured way immediately before it is called a weighty word, making disciplined tongue-bearing part of the burden image.
God knows what the earth diminishes of the dead, and with Him is a preserving Book; divine record safeguards what disappears from sight.
Had the Quran descended upon a mountain, it would have become humbled and split from fear of God; this gives revealed speech a figurative weight capable of crushing what bears it.
Believers are told not to turn their backs while hearing God and the Messenger, directly reversing the posture of audible revelation placed behind oneself.
The one who fears will take the reminder, supplying the receptive hearer for the Prophet's command to remind in 87:9.
The discourse is a clarification for humankind and guidance and admonition for the mindful, bringing bayān together with a reminder-like warning function.
God has brought a Book detailed with knowledge as guidance and mercy, another scriptural instance of revelation opened into explanation.
The Quran confirms prior revelation and provides a detailed exposition of the Book, linking faithful preservation with clarification.
The Book's verses are made firm and then set out in detail by One wise and aware, a movement from protected formulation into exposition.
The Book sent down is described as fully detailed, supporting the section's picture of scripture as an explanation rather than a concealed object.
The messengers convey God's messages and fear no one but Him, stating public delivery as the stance required of those entrusted with revelation.
On Judgment Day the rejecters cannot conceal any statement from God, marking the limit at which hidden speech must give way to disclosure.
What the deniers used to conceal becomes apparent to them, a reversal from hidden conduct to manifest recognition.
Secret speech and public speech, hiding by night and moving openly by day, are all alike to God; the verse expands the hidden-manifest polarity across word and movement.
Nothing hidden in heaven or earth lies outside a clear Book, joining concealment with comprehensive written preservation.
Nothing even of minute weight is hidden from God without being in a clear Book, making the record the place where the unseen remains present.
No deed escapes God even by an atom's weight, and all is in a clear Book; unnoticed action is preserved for manifestation.
Abraham addresses the One who knows what people conceal and disclose, placing hidden and open need before God in prayer.
The objects of worship say the people forgot the Reminder and became ruined, another explicit instance of revelation lost from active memory.
If Satan makes the hearer forget an instruction, remembrance requires leaving the wrongdoing company once recollection returns.
Everything people have done is preserved in written records, giving deeds a textual memory beyond human forgetting.
Every small and great deed is inscribed, completing 54:52 with the record's exhaustive scope.
At the upheaval each soul learns what it sent ahead and left behind, as formerly hidden conduct becomes present knowledge.
Guardians are appointed over people, beginning the explanation of how their acts remain preserved.
The guardians are noble recorders, making their protective oversight specifically an act of writing.
The recorders know what people do, completing the passage's account of deeds kept for disclosure.
The right-hand recipient says he knew he would meet his reckoning, contributing retained awareness to the openly displayed book scene of 69:19.
The left-hand recipient wishes he had not known his record, turning the manifest book into knowledge he longs to escape.
The Prophet is promised a praised station, an indirect form of divinely elevated honor that complements the raising of his public mention.
The command to mention Mary in the Book makes scripture itself the vehicle that keeps a person's story and name publicly remembered.
The repeated command to mention Abraham in the Book gives his truthful prophetic name an enduring textual presence.
Moses is likewise to be mentioned in the Book, showing scripture preserving a messenger's name and character.
Ishmael's mention in the Book continues the repeated pattern of prophetic names carried by revelation.
Idris is to be mentioned in the Book before his raised station is stated, joining scriptural remembrance to elevation across the two verses.
The Prophet is to remind with the Quran whoever fears the warning, making the Book the spoken instrument of recollection.
Opponents address the Prophet as the one to whom the Reminder was sent while accusing him of madness; even hostile speech identifies his public association with zikir.
The opponents ask whether the Reminder was sent specifically to this Prophet from among them, exposing their resentment at the distinction conferred by revelation.
